newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-MICKELSON, ELKINGTON OUT OF WORLD MATCHPLAY.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-MICKELSON, ELKINGTON OUT OF WORLD MATCHPLAY.

text.p: American Phil Mickelson and last year's runner-up Steve Elkington of Australia were upset in the opening round of the World Matchplay golf championship at Wentworth on Thursday.

Mickelson, the leader of the U.S. money list this year, dropped five of the first seven holes to Vijay Singh of Fiji, recovered to all square after 20 holes but then stumbled to a one-hole defeat on his debut in the event.
He almost forced a play-off. Bunkered beside the green in two at the 36th, Mickelson's sand shot flew straight into the hole but bounced out again and finished three feet away.
From off the green, Singh got up and down to preserve his victory with a four-foot birdie putt.
Elkington, beaten by Ernie Els in last year's final, led by two holes against American Steve Stricker after 18 holes but faded in the afternoon and went down 3 and 2.

Colin Montgomerie, winner of four successive European Orders of Merit, defeated two-times champion Ian Woosnam 3 and 2 in their all-British battle, while American Mark O'Meara crushed Japan's Nobuo Serizawa 7 and 5 in the other match.

The top four seeds all had byes. Top seed Els will face Stricker in Friday's second round, British Open champion Tom Lehman faces O'Meara, U.S. Open champion Steve Jones takes on Singh and PGA winner Mark Brooks meets Montgomerie.
Mickelson, the left-hander who has won four titles and $1.6 million this year, was left to rue his luck at the final hole.
"I can't believe the ball at the last came out of the hole, but then I guess it was lucky to fly in," said Mickelson, close to an eagle at the hole for the second time in the day.
"I hit a couple of poor drives coming in, at the 31st and 34th. I kind of gave him those holes without forcing him to make birdies," Mickelson said.

Singh was among those who thought Mickelson had holed his bunker shot. "I looked up and saw Phil's shot hit the hole," he said. "I expected him to make four and I just wanted to make sure I didn't make five."
Elkington, the 1995 PGA champion, led by two holes after the morning round against Stricker, courtesy of birdies at the 12th and 13th, but the 29-year-old American fought back after lunch.

Stricker, who won all five matches as the U.S. team which also included O'Meara and Mickelson, took the Alfred Dunhill Cup on Sunday, sealed his victory with birdies at the 30th and 32nd holes and won with a par at the 34th.
"In the afternoon I didn't have anything to lose and I got the speed of the greens a bit better," said Stricker, winner of the Kemper and Western Opens and fifth on the U.S. money list.
Montgomerie seized the lead from Woosnam at the 18th with a birdie and was four up with nine to play.
Woosnam, who blamed his putting and not his injured back, almost conceded on the 33rd green before realising the match was not quite over. He lost at the next.
"I thought there were only two holes to go, not three. I forgot where we were for a moment," he explained.
Montgomerie, like Singh, owed much to his form off the tee. He was outdriving Woosnam by an average 30 yards throughout the match.
O'Meara led Serizawa by two at lunch and did not drop a shot in the afternoon, making three birdies to storm to victory with a 12-foot birdie at the 31st.
"I've played Nobuo before and it seemed he has lost a bit of length. I wondered if he were injured," O'Meara said.
